title: Project Overview
description: Start with the README, which presents react-socket-link as a lightweight, TypeScript-first WebSocket library for React with hook-based APIs, auto-reconnect with exponential backoff, typed pub/sub messaging, and multi-connection management. It covers the quick start (wrap the app in WebSocketProvider with a connections map, then call useSubscription/useSend), static vs. dynamic connections, every hook, backoff strategies, and React Strict Mode behavior. Keep this mental map handy: the rest of the tour walks through the code behind each of these features.

title: Public Package Entry
description: src/index.ts is the single public surface of the package: it re-exports the WebSocketClient core, the React provider and hooks, the shared types, and the backoff utilities. It has the highest fan-out in the project, so reading its export list is the fastest way to see the library's architecture: a framework-agnostic core wrapped by a thin React layer. Every module visited in the following steps is reached directly from here.
languageLesson: A barrel file uses `export { ... } from './module'` and `export type { ... }` to re-export symbols, giving consumers one import path while keeping the internal file layout private. Type-only re-exports are erased at compile time and add no runtime cost.

title: Shared Type Vocabulary
description: Before reading any runtime code, learn the vocabulary in src/types/index.ts: the ConnectionState enum, the generic BaseMessage, handler and unsubscribe callback types, BackoffStrategy, and WebSocketClientOptions. This is the Types Layer imported by every other source module, which is why it ranks second in fan-in. BaseMessage underpins the typed messaging the README describes, where messages are discriminated by their type field so handlers receive precisely narrowed payloads.
languageLesson: Discriminated unions combine several object types that share a literal `type` field. TypeScript narrows the union when you check that field, and generics such as `Extract<TMessage, { type: K }>` let a subscription keyed by a type string receive exactly the matching message shape.

title: Reconnect Backoff Strategies
description: src/utils/Backoff.ts implements the BackoffStrategy type from Step 3 in two flavors: exponential backoff with full jitter, and a fixed-delay strategy. Each returns a function that computes the delay before the next reconnect attempt. Full jitter randomizes delays across the whole window so many clients that lose a server at once do not reconnect in a synchronized stampede.
languageLesson: Returning a function from a factory (a closure) lets callers configure settings such as base and max delay once, then reuse the captured values on every attempt without passing them again.

title: Core WebSocketClient
description: WebsocketClient.ts is the heart of the Core Client Layer: a generic, framework-agnostic client that manages connection lifecycle, reconnects using the backoff strategies from Step 4, sends heartbeats to detect dead connections, dispatches incoming messages to subscribers by message type, and queues outbound messages while disconnected so they flush on reconnect. Because it has no React dependency it can be used on its own, and the React layer in the next steps simply wraps it.
languageLesson: A generic class such as `WebSocketClient<TMessage extends BaseMessage>` threads one type parameter through every method, so subscribe, send and handler signatures all stay consistent with the message union the caller supplies.

title: WebSocketProvider Context
description: WebSocketProvider.tsx bridges the core client into React. It lazily creates and caches named WebSocketClient instances, either from a static connections map or through a resolve function for dynamic, pattern-based connections. It also handles React Strict Mode remounts and cleanup, so a development double-mount does not leave duplicate sockets behind.
languageLesson: React Context combined with a ref-held cache (for example a Map stored in useRef) is a common way to share long-lived, mutable objects such as sockets across a component tree without triggering re-renders when the cache changes.

title: The Hooks API
description: src/hooks/index.ts is what application components actually call: useWebSocket retrieves a named client from the provider in Step 6, useSubscription subscribes to a message type, useConnectionState tracks the ConnectionState from Step 3, useSend sends messages, useCloseClient closes a connection, and useDynamicConnection follows ID-based dynamic connections. Each hook is a thin adapter over the WebSocketClient from Step 5, turning imperative subscribe and unsubscribe calls into React-managed effects.
languageLesson: Custom hooks pair useEffect with a returned cleanup function: subscribing in the effect body and returning the unsubscribe callback guarantees handlers are removed when a component unmounts or its dependencies change.

title: Packaging and Build
description: With the source understood, see how it ships. package.json defines react-socket-link v0.1.0 with dual ESM/CJS dist exports, type declarations, and a React >=17 peer dependency. vite.config.ts builds the src/index.ts entry from Step 2 in library mode into ES and CJS bundles with bundled .d.ts files, externalizes React so the host app supplies it, and configures Vitest to run tests in jsdom.
languageLesson: The package.json `exports` field maps `import` and `require` conditions to separate ESM and CJS files plus a `types` entry, so both module systems and TypeScript resolve the correct artifact. Declaring React as a peer dependency and marking it external in the bundler avoids shipping a second copy of React.

title: TypeScript and Lint Tooling
description: The TypeScript configs split responsibilities: tsconfig.json enables strict mode for editor typechecking across src, tests and examples; tsconfig.build.json extends it to emit only .d.ts declarations from src (excluding tests) for the build in Step 8; and tsconfig.node.json covers Node-side tooling like vite.config.ts. eslint.config.js applies the recommended JS, typescript-eslint and React Hooks rule sets, which help keep the hooks from Step 7 correct.
languageLesson: TypeScript configs can inherit with `extends`, so a build-only config reuses the base compiler options while overriding `include`, `exclude` and emit settings such as declaration-only output.
